To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the nodal distance between two stimuli is the distance between the two stimuli in the chain of conditional relations that were used to establish the equivalence class.
equivalence class membership and the nodal structure within an equivalence class can be simultaneously present in the same class.

the relational properties expressed in a test trial are dependent on both the equivalence class and the format of the test trial, with the latter determining the nodal structure expressed by the stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and analysis of equivalence classes and with the development of a theory of equivalence relations.
the development of a theoretical framework for understanding equivalence class structure and the partition of such classes into functional sub-classes.
the development and analysis of equivalence relations and the role of the nodal structure in the development of such relations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nodal structure is not a property of equivalence classes but rather is the property of equivalence relations.

the relational properties of the stimuli in a class are determined by nodal structure when the format of the test trial allows more that one response option per equivalence class, but that the relational properties are determined by equivalence class membership when the format of a trial allows only one stimulus option per equivalence class.
the nodal structure and the functional partitioning of equivalence class membership are not mutually exclusive, but rather are determined by the format of the test trials.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the relational properties expressed in an equivalence class by the stimuli in that class depend upon the discriminative function of the format of a post-class-formation transfer test trial.
the stimuli in an established equivalence class can be functionally partitioned into subunits based on nodal structure, but only when a test procedure allows more than one option per class.
a functional equivalence class can be bifurcated in terms of nodality when the format of a transfer test trial is such that it allows multiple response options per class.
The main takeaway from our work is that
equivalence relations are not unitary.
a class is a class, but a class is not a class, which is to say that a class is more complex than we thought.
equivalence class formation is not an all-or-none process, but rather a process that is sensitive to the format of the test trials that are used to assess class membership.
